questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a fixed term of judicial office protects against
questions.stem: We began revision on judicial independence by asking what a fixed term of office actually protects a judge against.

options.text: It protects against the executive or legislature removing the judge to influence a case
It protects against the judge's own bias, since a term ends once doubts appear
options.misconception: assumes a fixed term removes personal bias

options.text: It protects the judge's salary, since pay is fixed for the duration of the term
options.misconception: confuses tenure protection with pay security

options.text: It protects against criticism of judgments by guaranteeing that silence continues
options.misconception: treats tenure as a shield against criticism

questions.explanation: A fixed term secures the judge's position so that removal pressure cannot be used to steer an outcome in a particular case. It does not remove personal bias, fix pay, or shield decisions from criticism.
questions.hint: Focus on removal pressure, not bias or pay.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define the access to justice gap
questions.stem: We compared court fee income with the numbers of claims brought, and the difference is what we mean by the access to justice gap.

options.text: The gap is the number of cases dismissed, since dismissal shows access failed
options.misconception: treats dismissal as the measure of access

options.text: The gap is the difference between people with a legal problem and those who can act on it
The gap is the shortfall in court funding compared with the budget set last year
options.misconception: confuses institutional underfunding with access

options.text: The gap is the time judges take to list cases, since delay delays every claimant
options.misconception: reduces access to a single procedural delay

questions.explanation: Access to justice is measured by whether people can bring and pursue a claim, so the gap lies between those with a problem and those able to act on it. Underfunding and delay are causes of the gap, not its definition.
questions.hint: Ask who can and cannot bring a claim.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what substantive equality requires of equal treatment
questions.stem: Our tutor asked whether treating everyone identically can still produce an unequal outcome, and we had to work out what substantive equality requires.

answer.exemplar: Substantive equality asks whether the rules produce equal results in practice, not merely whether they are worded identically. Identical treatment may leave a group behind where starting conditions, costs of participation or barriers to participation differ, so a measure may need to allocate extra resources or remove a barrier rather than apply the same treatment. The test is whether the legal framework enables people in comparable situations to compete and access the same opportunities.

questions.explanation: Substantive equality looks at outcomes and the barriers people actually face, not just identical wording of rules. It allows measures that treat groups differently where equal treatment would preserve an existing disadvantage.
questions.hint: Compare the treatment rule with the outcome it produces.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of complaints that reach investigation
questions.stem: The ombudsman received 1,240 complaints in the year and investigated 310 of them. What percentage of the complaints received were investigated?
questions.explanation: 310 divided by 1,240 is exactly 0.25, so 25 per cent of complaints were investigated. The remaining three quarters were resolved without a formal investigation, typically by explanation and advice.
questions.hint: Divide investigated complaints by all complaints.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the exhaustion requirement to a tribunal ruling

stimulus.body: The tribunal records that the claimant challenged the assessment before the internal review panel and was refused, and that no further appeal has been brought in respect of the same decision. The ruling notes that the matter may now proceed to the court.

questions.stem: Given this extract, what does the ruling require of the claimant before the court will hear the dispute?

options.text: Nothing further, because the internal panel decision was already a court judgment
options.misconception: treats an internal panel as a court

options.text: A second internal review, because one review never satisfies the requirement
options.misconception: assumes the same review must be repeated

options.text: That the internal remedy has been used, since the rule requires domestic remedies first
A settlement conference, because negotiation must precede any court hearing
options.misconception: inserts negotiation as a legal precondition

questions.explanation: The exhaustion rule requires a claimant to use available domestic remedies before turning to the court, and the extract shows the internal review was used. A settlement conference is a practical step, not a legal precondition.
questions.hint: Check whether the internal remedy was used.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Define what a court clearance rate measures
questions.stem: For the statistics session we worked out how to read a clearance rate, where the case disposal divided by the cases received is expressed as a percentage.

options.text: It shows the average time each case took, since faster disposal raises the rate
options.misconception: confuses a clearance rate with an average duration

options.text: It shows the proportion of judges who disposed of cases within a target time
options.misconception: reads the rate as a judge performance measure

options.text: It shows the number of cases pending, since a high rate means more waiting
options.misconception: inverts the relationship between rate and backlog

options.text: It shows the share of incoming cases disposed of, since disposal is set against receipts

questions.explanation: A clearance rate compares cases disposed of with cases received in the same period, so it measures whether the court is keeping pace with new work. It says nothing about case duration or about the backlog itself.
questions.hint: Compare disposal with receipts for the same period.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret re-opening of settlements in a tribunal caseload
questions.stem: Our notes record that a specialist tribunal heard 2,300 claims, that 700 were settled before hearing, and that 240 of the settled claims were later reopened by the same parties.

options.text: Reopening 240 of the 700 settlements suggests the settlements were not always final in practice
Reopening 240 of the 700 settlements shows the tribunal wrongly refused to hear cases
options.misconception: reads reopening as proof of wrongful refusal

options.text: Reopening 240 of the 700 settlements proves the settlements exceeded the tribunal's powers
options.misconception: presumes every settlement was void

options.text: Reopening 240 of the 700 settlements indicates a rise in applications to the tribunal
options.misconception: mistakes re-opening of old claims for new demand

questions.explanation: Re-opening 240 of the 700 settlements, about a third, shows the settlements did not hold in practice, which points to the quality of the agreement rather than to the tribunal's jurisdiction. It is not evidence of wrongful refusal or of new demand.
questions.hint: Compare reopened settlements with all settlements.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the conditions that make negotiated justice legitimate
questions.stem: We argued about negotiated justice, where an offender and victim agree a remedy without a contested trial, and asked when that is legitimate.

answer.exemplar: Negotiated justice is legitimate where the process is voluntary on both sides, the offender accepts responsibility, the victim is properly supported and informed, and the agreement is reviewed against the public interest. The concerns are real: pressure from the state or the family can make consent hollow, and a private agreement cannot be allowed to deny a remedy that the public interest requires. Safeguards such as independent support and judicial or prosecutorial approval limit that risk.

questions.explanation: Negotiated justice is defensible where consent is genuinely informed and the outcome is reviewed against the public interest. Coercion of the victim and privately negotiated denial of a public remedy are the main risks.
questions.hint: Ask whether the consent is informed and voluntary.

questions.topic: Conceptions of the rule of law
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the difference between two rule of law index scores
questions.stem: A rule of law index scored the country 0.72 on a scale from zero to one, and a comparator scored 0.48. What is the difference between the two scores?
questions.explanation: 0.72 minus 0.48 is 0.24, so the gap between the two scores is 0.24 points on the zero to one scale. The index compresses many institutional features into one number, so a gap of this size indicates relative strength rather than any absolute guarantee.
questions.hint: Subtract the lower score from the higher one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify judicialization from a description of shifting decision-making

stimulus.body: The note observes that over the decade a growing share of disputes that previously ended in quiet administrative negotiation were brought before a court, and that senior officials describe referring decisions upward as the normal way to secure a defensible outcome.

questions.stem: What does this note describe, and what does it suggest about how disputes are now settled?

options.text: It describes de-judicialization, because decisions are being settled outside the courts
options.misconception: reads upward referral as informal settlement

options.text: It describes judicialization, because decisions are increasingly made through formal legal process
It describes legal inflation, because officials are inflating the value of their decisions
options.misconception: confuses judicialization with inflating the stakes

options.text: It describes procedural reform, because the rules for referring cases have changed
options.misconception: assumes a procedural rule change is the cause

questions.explanation: Judicialization describes the shift of decision-making from informal administrative negotiation into formal legal process. Officials seeking a defensible outcome by referring cases upward is a symptom of that shift, not a reform of procedure.
questions.hint: Ask where decisions are now being made.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether independence survives a dependent reappointment
questions.stem: One of us asked whether judicial independence survives if a judge's reappointment depends on the satisfaction of the government making the appointment.

options.text: It does survive, because a fixed term already secures the judge's position
options.misconception: assumes a fixed term neutralises appointment power

options.text: It survives, because reappointment is a matter for the judiciary alone
options.misconception: assumes judges control their own reappointment

options.text: It is weakened, because a dependent reappointment can be used to influence decisions
It does not survive at all, because any external appointment defeats independence
options.misconception: treats any external appointment as fatal

questions.explanation: Independence depends on the absence of incentives that could sway a decision. If reappointment turns on governmental satisfaction, judges face a real pressure even with a fixed term, so the arrangement weakens independence without abolishing it.
questions.hint: Consider the incentive created at renewal.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a legal right does not deliver equal access to justice
questions.stem: We were asked to explain why the existence of a right to bring proceedings does not by itself mean that access to justice is equal.

answer.exemplar: Formal availability of proceedings is only the starting point for access to justice. Cost, legal knowledge, travel, language, fear of the other party and the length of delay all affect whether a person can realistically use a remedy, and these burdens fall unevenly across groups. Equal access therefore requires attention to those practical barriers, such as legal aid, simplified procedures and interpreters, not merely a statute that provides a cause of action and a court to bring it in.

questions.explanation: A legal right to sue can be unusable where cost, distance or lack of knowledge blocks access, and those barriers fall unevenly. Equal access therefore requires practical supports as well as a formal cause of action.
questions.hint: Distinguish a legal right from its practical use.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of applicants from lower-income households
questions.stem: In the equality scenario, 4,000 applications were received for a bursary, 3,200 came from households with an annual income below 20,000, and 1,200 came from households above that income. What percentage of applicants came from households below the threshold?
questions.explanation: 3,200 divided by 4,000 is exactly 0.80, so 80 per cent of applicants came from households below the threshold. Identical treatment would distribute the limited bursary money across applicants regardless of whether the need was the same in degree.
questions.hint: Divide applicants below the threshold by all applicants.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of complaints closed without investigation

stimulus.body: The annual report records that the ombudsman received 4,800 complaints, of which 3,100 were closed after investigation and recommendations, 900 were closed without investigation, and the remainder were carried forward to the following year.

questions.stem: According to this report, what proportion of the complaints received were closed without an investigation?

options.text: About 36 per cent, because 1,700 of the complaints were closed in that way
options.misconception: mislabels the carried-forward cases as closed

options.text: About 65 per cent, because 3,100 complaints were closed after investigation
options.misconception: reports the investigated share as the uninvestigated one

options.text: Exactly 100 per cent, because every complaint eventually closed
options.misconception: ignores the cases carried forward

options.text: About 19 per cent, because 900 of the 4,800 complaints were closed without investigation

questions.explanation: 900 divided by 4,800 is 0.1875, which is about 19 per cent of the complaints received. The 800 carried forward were not closed at all, so they cannot be counted as closed without investigation.
questions.hint: Compare the uninvestigated closures with all complaints.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose and effect of the exhaustion rule
questions.stem: A question came up on why the exhaustion rule exists and what happens if a claimant skips the domestic stage.

options.text: It saves court time by letting domestic bodies settle disputes first, and premature filing is refused
It exists so that courts can check the quality of domestic decisions before ruling
options.misconception: reverses the purpose of screening disputes

options.text: It exists because domestic decisions are presumed final and cannot be questioned later
options.misconception: assumes domestic decisions are unreviewable

options.text: It exists to give the domestic body time to correct its own procedural mistakes
options.misconception: reduces the rule to a cure for procedural errors

questions.explanation: The exhaustion rule screens disputes through domestic bodies first, conserving court time and allowing local remedies to operate. A claimant who goes straight to court without using the available remedy is generally expected to use it first.
questions.hint: Consider who is expected to try the dispute first.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compute a clearance rate from annual court figures
questions.stem: The court figures for the year show 5,400 cases received, 5,150 disposed of, and 250 disposed of within 20 working days of allocation.

options.text: The clearance rate is 95 per cent, because 5,150 is a little under 5,400
options.misconception: rounds a shortfall rate into a disposal rate

options.text: The clearance rate is about 95 per cent, since disposal is measured against receipts
The clearance rate is 105 per cent, because 5,150 exceeds 5,400 once rounded
options.misconception: inverts the ratio between disposal and receipts

options.text: The clearance rate is 4.6 per cent, because 250 cases moved quickly
options.misconception: uses the fast-track count as the clearance rate

questions.explanation: 5,150 disposed of against 5,400 received is roughly 95.4 per cent, so the court is keeping pace with new work. The figure for cases moved within 20 days measures speed on a small subset and is not the clearance rate.
questions.hint: Set disposal against receipts for the same year.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the rationale for and limits of administrative tribunals
questions.stem: We had to explain to the group why administrative tribunals were set up instead of asking people to use the ordinary courts for similar disputes.

answer.exemplar: Administrative tribunals exist because the ordinary courts are not well suited to certain classes of dispute. They can be given specialist decision-makers, simplified procedures, flexible evidence rules and lower costs, and they can sit close to the industry or public service concerned. That expertise and accessibility can improve the quality of decisions for the parties. The concern is independence and accountability, which is why procedural fairness, published reasons and avenues of appeal to the courts are built into the scheme.

questions.explanation: Tribunals offer expertise, speed and lower cost for disputes unsuited to ordinary courts, which can improve decisions for users. Their independence and accountability then depend on fair procedure, published reasons and appeal to the courts.
questions.hint: Ask what specialisation buys and what it risks.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Conceptions of the rule of law
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many countries fall short of advance publication of laws
questions.stem: In the rule of law survey, 25 of 40 countries published their laws in advance of taking effect, and 30 of 40 had courts that enforced decisions against the executive. How many of the 40 countries failed to publish laws in advance of taking effect?
questions.explanation: 40 minus 25 leaves 15 countries that did not publish laws in advance, which is 37.5 per cent of the sample. Advance publication is one element of legality, and the rule of law depends on several such elements together.
questions.hint: Subtract the compliant countries from the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess decision-making that bypasses formal legal process

stimulus.body: The minute records the chair's concern that a dispute between the agency and the supplier was settled by a negotiated payment outside the published procedure, and the note that the legal department had not been asked to advise before the agreement was signed.

questions.stem: What does this minute suggest about the shift of decision-making into negotiation?

options.text: It suggests a return to informal justice, which is typical of a mature legal system
options.misconception: assumes informal settlement is necessarily a sign of maturity

options.text: It suggests the ordinary procedure was unavailable, which explains the negotiation
options.misconception: presumes necessity where the minute records none

options.text: It suggests judicialization being avoided, or displaced, when decisions leave formal process
It suggests the legal department resisted involvement, so the agency acted alone
options.misconception: assigns resistance not mentioned in the minute

questions.explanation: When a dispute is settled outside the published procedure and legal advice is skipped, decision-making is being displaced from formal legal process rather than simply kept out of court. The minute records no reason why the procedure could not be used, and no resistance by the legal department.
questions.hint: Focus on where the decision was made.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the gap across multiple access barriers
questions.stem: Someone in the group asked what counts as the access to justice gap when fees are reduced but waiting times rise.

options.text: The gap narrows automatically, because lower fees always improve access
options.misconception: assumes cost is the only barrier that matters

options.text: The gap is unchanged, because access is measured only by fee levels
options.misconception: reduces access to a single variable

options.text: The gap widens only if fees rise, since fees are the binding constraint
options.misconception: identifies fees as the only relevant constraint

options.text: The gap must be measured across cost, delay, distance and information, not fees alone

questions.explanation: Access to justice is multi-dimensional: cost, delay, distance and information all matter. Reducing fees while lengthening waits may not improve access at all, so the gap has to be assessed on several measures together.
questions.hint: Consider all the barriers at once.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare the ombudsman with a court and explain the difference in remedy
questions.stem: We were asked how an ombudsman differs from a court and why the difference in the remedy matters for complainants.

answer.exemplar: An ombudsman investigates complaints against public authorities and may recommend a remedy, but in most systems it cannot compel compliance and its recommendations are not enforceable in the way a court order is. Its value lies in accessibility, informality, costlessness and speed, and in its ability to report on patterns of poor administration across agencies. For complainants, that means a realistic route to correction and explanation without litigation, alongside the limitation that an unsuccessful recommendation may leave the underlying grievance unresolved.

questions.explanation: An ombudsman offers an accessible and low cost route to investigate maladministration and to recommend correction, but typically cannot enforce its recommendations. That distinction explains both its usefulness and the residual limitation for complainants.
questions.hint: Compare compulsory enforcement with recommendation.

questions.stem: In the negotiated justice scenario, 90 of the 120 cases in the sample were resolved by agreement and the other 30 by contested hearing. What percentage of cases were resolved by agreement rather than a contested hearing?
questions.explanation: 90 divided by 120 is exactly 0.75, so 75 per cent of cases in the sample were resolved by agreement. A high share prompts questions about voluntariness and about whether some cases are being diverted from open testing of the facts.
questions.hint: Divide agreed cases by the total number of cases.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the provision that most protects a judge from removal pressure

stimulus.body: The regulation provides that a serving judge holds office for a fixed term, may be removed only for defined misconduct, and that a salary determined by law shall be paid and may not be varied to the disadvantage of the holder during the term.

questions.stem: Which feature of this regulation does most to protect the judge in the exercise of judicial function?

options.text: The bar on removing a judge except for defined misconduct, which blunts pressure to please
The fixed term itself, which guarantees that no appointment can ever be renewed
options.misconception: assumes a fixed term prevents reappointment

options.text: The salary rule, which protects the judge from any loss of income
options.misconception: treats pay protection as the core guarantee

options.text: The requirement to define misconduct, which shows the removal power is open-ended
options.misconception: reverses the effect of defining misconduct

questions.explanation: Independence depends on the judge's position not being vulnerable to removal as the price of an unwelcome decision. A closed list of misconduct and a secure salary remove those levers, while a fixed term alone leaves reappointment as a possible source of pressure.
questions.hint: Ask what makes removal impossible for displeasure.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the futility exception to the exhaustion requirement
questions.stem: Our tutor asked what a court should do when the domestic remedy exists but the claimant says it would be useless, and we compared the options.

options.text: The court must always refuse the case, because the rule has no exceptions at all
options.misconception: assumes the exhaustion rule has no flexibility

options.text: The court may consider whether pursuing the domestic remedy would be futile or pointless
The court must hear the case, because the domestic stage is merely advisory
options.misconception: assumes the domestic stage carries no binding effect

options.text: The court must wait for the domestic body to decide, since only it can judge its own process
options.misconception: denies the court any evaluative role

questions.explanation: Courts recognise that compliance with the exhaustion rule can be excused where the domestic remedy is unavailable or would be futile, otherwise the rule would deny access without purpose. The court still assesses the claim, but it does not automatically hear it.
questions.hint: Consider what happens if the remedy is useless.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish formally equal rules from substantively equal outcomes
questions.stem: We compared two grant schemes and found that 60 per cent of awards under the first went to the group with the highest average income, while under the second the awards tracked need.

options.text: The first scheme is identical in its treatment, so it must be equal on its face
options.misconception: confuses identical wording with equal outcome

options.text: The second scheme discriminates, because it treats the two groups differently
options.misconception: mistakes differential provision for discrimination

options.text: The first scheme is formally equal but substantively unequal, because identical rules reproduced prior advantage
Neither scheme can be assessed, because outcomes never show equal treatment
options.misconception: denies that outcome evidence bears on equality

questions.explanation: Substantive equality examines outcomes, and the first scheme applied identical rules to groups whose starting positions differed, so the advantage persisted. Differential treatment in the second scheme pursues equal outcomes rather than causing discrimination.
questions.hint: Ask whether identical rules produced equal results.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a clearance rate above one hundred signifies
questions.stem: The group debated why a court might dispose of more cases than it receives, and what follows if that pattern persists.

answer.exemplar: Disposing of more cases than arrive means the court is reducing its stock of pending work, which is the arithmetic definition of a clearance rate above one hundred. The causes usually combine: a surge of extra judges, a procedural reform that shortens cases, and administrative measures that push cases towards settlement or away from the formal list. Sustained clearance above one hundred is generally welcome because it shrinks waiting times, but only if the quality of decisions and the fairness of the process are not being sacrificed to speed.

questions.explanation: A clearance rate above one hundred means pending work is shrinking rather than growing, and sustained clearance usually shortens waiting times. That welcome result holds only if quality and fairness are not traded away for speed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the backlog is growing or shrinking.

questions.explanation: 550 divided by 800 is 0.6875, so 68.75 per cent of the appeals were withdrawn. A withdrawal rate that high suggests that the list of withdrawn appeals may include cases that would otherwise have been pursued, which affects how the disposal figures are read.

questions.learningObjective: Assess fairness concerns in negotiated sentencing data

questions.stem: What does this note suggest about the fairness of negotiated sentencing in the sample?

options.misconception: infers outcome bias from a single statistic

options.text: The sentences were shorter because the offences were less serious in those cases
options.misconception: assumes seriousness differs between the two groups

options.text: The results show that negotiated sentencing has no effect on sentence length
options.misconception: reads a difference as no effect

options.text: The shorter sentences and unrepresented victims together raise questions about informed consent and parity

questions.explanation: Shorter sentences in negotiated cases combined with victims lacking a representative raise two linked concerns: that consent may not be fully informed and that outcomes may not be comparable to contested cases. Neither point can be settled from sentence length alone.
questions.hint: Weigh the sentence comparison with the representation point.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish institutional from personal judicial independence
questions.stem: We turned to what judicial independence means in practice, and to the difference between the independence of a court and of the individual judge.

options.text: Institutional independence secures the court as an institution, while personal independence secures the individual judge

options.misconception: reverses the two meanings of independence

options.text: Both phrases describe the same thing, since a court is only a group of its judges
options.misconception: assumes institution and person are interchangeable

options.text: Personal independence protects the judge from criticism, while institutional independence protects the court's decisions
options.misconception: reduces independence to immunity from criticism

questions.explanation: Institutional independence concerns the court's position within the state, including its funding and the scope of its jurisdiction, while personal independence concerns the autonomy of the individual judge. A court can be institutionally secure while a particular judge remains vulnerable.
questions.hint: Distinguish the court from the person judging.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the proportion of people with a legal problem left unserved
questions.stem: The access survey found that 9,000 people with a legal problem in the region did not seek advice, while 3,000 did seek it and were helped.

options.text: Advice reached 25 per cent of those with a problem, because 3,000 of 12,000 sought it
options.misconception: treats the surveyed group as all people with problems

options.text: Most people with a legal problem went unserved, since 9,000 did not seek advice
Advice reached 75 per cent of those with a problem, because 9,000 went unhelped

questions.explanation: Of the 12,000 people with a legal problem, only 3,000 sought advice, so 9,000 or 75 per cent went without it, which is the access to justice gap. Advice-seeking and legal need are different things, but the survey reports need alongside use.
questions.hint: Add the two groups before taking a percentage.

options.misconception: assumes tribunals never hear witnesses

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a formally neutral rule can operate as a barrier
questions.stem: We had to write about how a formally neutral rule can operate as a barrier, using the example of a service that required people to apply online.

answer.exemplar: A rule that offers a single channel can be neutral on its face and still operate as a barrier when some people lack the access, the devices, the literacy or the time to use it. Neutrality of form is therefore not the same as equality of effect, and a service that insists on one channel effectively allocates inconvenience to those least able to bear it. The practical response is to provide alternatives, such as an offline route, assisted access or a phone option, so that the burden of the rule is not concentrated on one group.

questions.explanation: A single-channel rule imposes a real burden on people who cannot use that channel, so formal neutrality does not produce equal effect. Providing alternative routes is what removes the barrier rather than merely describing it.
questions.hint: Consider who cannot use the single channel.

options.misconception: overstates the protection a fixed term provides

options.text: That a reappointment or confirmation stage gives the appointing body a possible lever over a judge
That both designs are equivalent, since retirement age fixes the end of service
options.misconception: treats the two designs as producing the same incentives

options.text: That tenure has no bearing on independence, which rests only on the quality of reasoning
options.misconception: reduces independence to reasoning alone

questions.explanation: A non-renewable appointment closes off the reappointment lever, while a confirmation stage leaves the appointing body able to signal approval or disapproval of a judge. Both designs preserve an end point, but only one removes the future decision point entirely.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the decision at the end of service.

options.misconception: assumes finality removes the victim's interest

options.text: The victim can reopen the case alone, because the victim's consent is always revocable
options.misconception: overstates the victim's unilateral power to reopen

options.text: The victim's concern may be addressed through support, review and the usual appeal routes
The agreement is void automatically, because negotiated terms must satisfy the sentencing court
options.misconception: assumes negotiated cases are void without an objection raised

questions.explanation: A negotiated outcome is not simply void because one participant feels it was harsh; the response lies in support, independent review of the terms and the ordinary routes of challenge. The settlement binds in practice, so concerns must be raised through the proper mechanism.

options.misconception: reads raw disposal totals as the clearance rate

options.text: The clearance rate was unchanged, because both years disposed of more than nine in ten of receipts
options.misconception: misses the difference between the two years' rates

options.text: The two years cannot be compared, because they covered different volumes of business
options.misconception: claims the two years cannot be normalised

options.text: The clearance rate rose, from 90 per cent of receipts to 95 per cent in the second year

questions.explanation: In the first year 7,290 against 8,100 is exactly 90 per cent, and in the second 8,075 against 8,500 is exactly 95 per cent. The rate therefore rose, and the ratio rather than the raw total is what shows it.
questions.hint: Compute each year's disposal against its receipts.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why delay is itself an access to justice problem
questions.stem: We discussed why delay is treated as an access to justice problem in its own right and not merely an administrative inconvenience.

answer.exemplar: Delay denies a remedy at the moment it is needed. A person whose employment, housing or liberty is in dispute cannot use the remedy they are entitled to while the case waits, and the pressure that delay creates falls hardest on those with the least capacity to wait. Delay also compounds inequality, because those who can afford to pursue a case vigorously do better than those who cannot, and it drives parties into settlement whatever the merits. Treating delay as an access problem therefore shifts attention to the design of the process, not only to the volume of work.

questions.explanation: Delay denies effective access to the remedy, and the pressure of waiting falls unequally, so it affects both the timing and the fairness of outcomes. It also encourages settlement regardless of merit, which is why it belongs in access analysis.
questions.hint: Ask what a party loses while a case waits.

It simply awards compensation to the complainant and takes no view on the underlying process
options.misconception: reduces the ombudsman's role to compensation alone

options.text: It passes the complaint to the council's oversight committee without making any findings
options.misconception: assumes the ombudsman merely refers complaints on

options.text: It enforces the published timescale by issuing an order that the council must comply with
options.misconception: assumes the ombudsman can enforce its recommendations

questions.explanation: The ombudsman looks at the repeated failure as well as the individual harm, so it recommends a remedy for the applicant and a reporting change for the council. Its recommendations are not orders, so enforcement depends on the authority's response.
questions.hint: Look at both the remedy and the practice change.

options.text: The appeal is a second trial on the facts, in which new evidence may be heard
options.misconception: describes the appeal as a fresh trial on the facts

options.text: The appeal is generally limited to questions of law, with the tribunal keeping the facts
The appeal transfers the original claim to the court without any new hearing
options.misconception: assumes the appeal is a transfer of the claim

options.text: The appeal replaces the tribunal's decision automatically, unless the tribunal is reversed
options.misconception: misdescribes the effect of a successful appeal

questions.explanation: Appeals from tribunals are usually confined to questions of law, so the tribunal retains responsibility for the facts and the appeal corrects legal error rather than re-litigating the dispute. That division keeps the process proportionate and preserves the tribunal's specialist role.
questions.hint: Ask whether the appeal re-examines the facts.

options.misconception: assumes the total number of disputes explains the share

The figures show no change, because a 17 point difference is too small to indicate a trend
options.misconception: treats a measured difference as too small to matter

questions.explanation: A rise in the share of disputes ending in court or tribunal, from 61 to 78 per cent, is the pattern judicialization produces as more decisions move from informal negotiation into formal process. The change is large enough to indicate a direction of travel over a decade.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the appearance of independence is not sufficient
questions.stem: We had to explain why the appearance of independence is not enough and how an apparently independent decision can still be vulnerable.

answer.exemplar: Independence has an institutional and a personal dimension, and both matter for how decisions are made. A court may sit outside the executive and hold a secure budget, yet a judge who faces reappointment on the approval of the body that appointed them has a personal incentive that an outsider cannot see. Likewise, a decision may be lawfully made and reasoned in public while the forum in which it was made was chosen for political convenience. The safeguard is structural: fixed terms, closed grounds of removal, protected tenure and published reasons that allow the reader to check the reasoning independently.

questions.explanation: Institutional safeguards and personal incentives both bear on independence, so an outward appearance of separateness does not remove invisible pressures on a judge. The answer lies in structural protections such as secure tenure and published reasoning.
questions.hint: Look for incentives that an outsider cannot see.

options.text: That the safeguards are unnecessary, since the court retains the final say over sentence
options.misconception: assumes judicial approval alone cures any defects in consent

options.text: That the scheme works because the facilitator has the authority to impose the outcome
options.misconception: misdescribes the facilitator's role as coercive

options.text: That the safeguards lie in the separate preparation, which prevents any pressure at the meeting
options.misconception: overstates what preparation can guarantee

options.text: That preparation, independent facilitation and judicial approval together protect the consent process

questions.explanation: Legitimacy rests on a combination: separate preparation so each party is ready, facilitation so the discussion is not dominated, and judicial approval so the outcome is checked against the public interest. None of those elements works on its own, which is why the scheme uses all three.
questions.hint: Consider each safeguard separately and together.

options.text: It gets wrong that full formal testing is always better, because the resources and time are drawn from other cases
It gets wrong that courts are unsuitable for disputes, since they apply law accurately in every case
options.misconception: overstates the competence of ordinary courts

options.text: It gets wrong that judicialization is irreversible, since governments can always reverse the trend
options.misconception: assumes the trend can be reversed at will

options.text: It gets wrong that informal negotiation is unfair, since negotiation works better for every type of dispute
options.misconception: generalises the strengths of negotiation to all cases

questions.explanation: Sending every disagreement to formal test consumes court capacity, delays those cases and diverts attention from enforcing existing decisions. The criticism of judicialization concerns resource allocation and decision quality, not the competence of the courts.
questions.hint: Consider what formal testing costs the wider system.

options.misconception: assumes the internal stage carries no legal significance

options.text: Only the first is likely to be heard, since the second has not used the available remedy
Only the second is likely to be heard, since the internal review is an unreasonable delay
options.misconception: assumes a claim is prejudiced by using the remedy

options.text: Both claims are likely to fail, since courts cannot review administrative decisions
options.misconception: denies the availability of review at all

questions.explanation: The exhaustion rule directs the second claimant to the internal review, and the court would ordinarily expect that step to be taken before proceedings. Using the remedy is not a disadvantage, so the first claimant's position is stronger.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Conceptions of the rule of law
questions.learningObjective: Compare thin and thick conceptions of the rule of law
questions.stem: Our seminar asked us to compare a thin and a thick conception of the rule of law, and to say which one the data on courts and officials reflects.

answer.exemplar: A thin conception treats the rule of law as the regular exercise of public authority through general rules that apply equally, without retrospective legislation, arbitrary enforcement or the seizure of property outside lawful procedure. A thick conception adds the substantive claim that the laws themselves should protect the dignity and equality of individuals, so that a state may have general laws yet still fall short. Statistical work on published laws, official discretion and access to courts usually captures the thin dimensions, while the thick dimensions appear in measures of equality, due process for individuals and the treatment of vulnerable groups.

questions.explanation: The thin conception covers predictable, general and impartially applied rules, while the thick conception adds that the laws must themselves uphold dignity and equality. Published laws and official discretion indicators track the thin dimensions, so a good score there does not settle the thick question.
questions.hint: Ask which dimensions the indicators actually capture.

options.text: It is part of the rule of law, since every recommendation carries the force of a court order
options.misconception: overstates the binding force of recommendations

It has no bearing on the rule of law, because complaints are too informal to matter
options.misconception: dismisses informal avenues as legally irrelevant

questions.explanation: Making official decisions answerable to complaint and review is part of what the rule of law does in practice, so an accessible complaints route strengthens rather than displaces it. The ombudsman's recommendations are not court orders, so its value lies in accessibility and scrutiny.

options.misconception: mistakes differential treatment for discrimination

options.misconception: treats consistency as a complete test of equality

options.text: The first scheme is equal in form but unequal in effect, since need was distributed unevenly

questions.explanation: Applying a rule consistently is not the same as achieving equality, and allocating by application date allowed the better-off households to capture most of the benefit. The need-based scheme pursues substantive equality by treating differently where the situations differ.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the jurisdictional distinction between tribunals and courts
questions.stem: We were asked why a distinction is drawn between the jurisdiction of administrative tribunals and the courts, and what follows from it.

answer.exemplar: Tribunals are given a defined jurisdiction that is narrower than the courts' and is usually confined to a particular sector or subject, with a statutory right of appeal to the courts on questions of law. The distinction keeps routine disputes away from the general court system, where procedure and cost are heavier, and lets tribunals use decision-makers with relevant expertise and more flexible procedure. It also creates a boundary that must be policed, since a decision outside the tribunal's jurisdiction may be a nullity and a fresh application may be needed, so parties often face two stages before reaching a court.

questions.explanation: The narrower jurisdiction and the right of appeal structure the system, keeping routine disputes out of the general courts while preserving a route to a court for legal error. The boundary also creates jurisdictional risk for parties who go to the wrong forum.
questions.hint: Consider what the narrower jurisdiction buys and costs.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the statutory allocation rule between forums

options.text: The allocation rule sends defined categories to the tribunal, so the forum follows the subject matter rather than preference
The allocation rule is a matter of convenience for the parties, who may opt for either forum

options.text: The allocation rule ensures consistent outcomes, so cases always reach the same result

options.text: The allocation rule is only administrative, since both bodies may deal with any dispute
options.misconception: assumes the jurisdictions overlap without limit

questions.explanation: A statutory allocation rule defines which claims belong with the tribunal and which with the courts, so the forum follows the legal character of the dispute rather than any party's preference. A claim filed in the wrong forum may be transferred, but the boundary is a legal rule rather than an administrative convenience.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an ombudsman achieves results without enforcement power
questions.stem: We had to explain how an ombudsman investigation can achieve results without being able to compel anything, and why that is a strength rather than a defect.

answer.exemplar: An ombudsman cannot enforce its recommendations, so its leverage comes from the reputational and legal exposure a public report creates, from the clarity of the findings, and from the political cost of ignoring a published recommendation. Because it is free, independent and informal, people use it who would never begin proceedings, so it reaches a population that courts do not. Its recommendations then become evidence of the standard expected of a public authority, and patterns across complaints support wider reform of administrative practice.

questions.explanation: Without enforcement power the ombudsman relies on publicity, credibility and the cost of non-compliance, which works because it is free, independent and accessible to people who would not litigate. Its value lies in reach and in the pattern of findings that drive administrative reform.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when a recommendation is ignored.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Conceptions of the rule of law
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the mean score across dimensions of the rule of law
questions.stem: The monitoring framework tracks four dimensions of the rule of law, and the country scored 0.80, 0.55, 0.70 and 0.35 on them. What is the mean of the four scores?
questions.explanation: The four scores total 2.40, and 2.40 divided by four is 0.60, so the mean score is 0.60. Averaging hides the spread, since the weakest dimension is 0.35 while the strongest is 0.80, and shortfalls in one area cannot be made good by strength in another.
questions.hint: Add the four scores and divide by four.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Name judicialization and assess its significance for the rule of law

stimulus.body: The extract notes that the increase in litigation coincided with a rise in requests for judicial review of administrative decisions, and that senior officials now routinely seek a court's ruling before taking decisions they once considered routine.

questions.stem: What is the best description of this pattern and its significance for the rule of law?

options.text: It describes judicial conservatism, because officials have become more cautious in general
options.misconception: reads greater use of courts as simple timidity

options.text: It describes the disappearance of discretion, because no administrative decision is now made at all
options.misconception: infers an absence of discretion from the use of review

options.text: It describes judicialization, and it may strengthen legality by subjecting decisions to independent scrutiny
It describes a decline in administrative capacity, because officials can no longer act alone
options.misconception: assumes the pattern is evidence of administrative failure

questions.explanation: The shift of decisions into court and review proceedings is judicialization, and it can improve legality by subjecting administrative choices to independent, published reasoning. The cost is capacity diverted to defending and avoiding decisions, and the benefit is not automatic where courts are also overloaded.
questions.hint: Name the pattern first, then weigh its effect.
